newsitem.title: UK: Southern Electric plans link up.
newsitem.headline: Southern Electric plans link up.

text.p: Southern Electric Plc, one of Britain's two surviving independent regional electricity companies (Recs), wants to tackle liberalisation of the market in 1998 by linking up with one or more national brand names, company officials said.
"Southern is not a known brand in the north of England, where, for example, a supermarket or petrol company might be," Ralph Earwicker, director of corporate relations, told Reuters in an interview.
The electricity industry in Britain will start to open fully to competition in steps from April 1998 when domestic customers should be able to pick suppliers.
After a flurry of takeovers in the last two years, Southern and Yorkshire Electricity are the only two Recs remaining independent of the 12 set up at privatisation in 1990.
Southern plans to stay independent and has no aims for any corporate activity such as acquisitions ahead of a general election, which must be held by May 1997.
"The focus is on our four key businesses -- distribution, supply, generation and contracting," Earwicker said.
Distribution accounts for some 70-75 percent of the company's profits, he said, with the remaining three sectors contributing around seven percent each.
"But those three are growing," Earwicker said.

The company has suffered from industry concern that it lacked direction after its plans to link up with generator National Power and take over its local water supplier, Southern Water, were thwarted last year.
The government blocked National Power's planned takeover in April 1996 and Scottish Power won control of Southern Water after Southern Electric dropped out of the bidding last summer.
It compensated shareholders with plans for returning value early this year that could add up to 156 million pounds ($250 million).
Southern now aims to build more independent power plants (IPPs) to add to the interest it already has in three stations.
In addition, it would like to clinch further deals for electricity supplies following last November's agreement with nuclear generator British Energy for supplies for up to 15 years or more.
Southern wants both to defend existing customers and fight for more after the electricity market is opened up, officials said.
It is currently staging a huge investment programme in its network, aimed at cutting downtime for customers and proving its reliability as a supplier.
Southern is spending 130 million pounds a year upgrading its rural transmission networks, switching existing overhead cables to more resilient products, director of distribution Colin Hood said.
Around 5,000 km of a total 15,000 km of network should be upgraded over five years, he said.
The work should reduce cutouts to customers by 50 percent, affecting 900,000 of Southern's 2.6 million users.
In addition, work is under way to improve urban distribution systems with automation and cable improvements which could affect a further one million customers, he said.
"I think the City is beginning to see where our strategy leads," Earwicker said. ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
